title: Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease with a Mediterranean Diet Supplemented with Extra-Virgin Olive Oil or Nuts
authors: Estruch R, Ros E, Salas-Salvadó J, Covas MI, Corella D, Arós F, et al.
followUp: median 4.8 years (interquartile range 2.8 to 5.8); stopped at the fourth prespecified interim analysis
population: Men aged 55 to 80 years and women aged 60 to 80 years in Spain without cardiovascular disease, with type 2 diabetes or at least three major cardiovascular risk factors; 11 sites with 169 clinics
funder: Instituto de Salud Carlos III, Spanish Ministry of Health (RTIC G03/140, RTIC RD 06/0045, CIBEROBN); Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares; Fondo de Investigación Sanitaria–Fondo Europeo de Desarrollo Regional; Ministerio de Ciencia e Innovación; Fundación Mapfre 2010; Consejería de Salud de la Junta de Andalucía; Public Health Division of the Department of Health of the Autonomous Government of Catalonia; Generalitat Valenciana; Regional Government of Navarra; Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute grant to one author. None of the sponsors had any role in the study design, data analysis, or reporting of the results.
inKindSupport: Extra virgin olive oil donated by Hojiblanca and Patrimonio Comunal Olivarero; walnuts by the California Walnut Commission; almonds by Borges; hazelnuts by Morella Nuts.
authorConflicts: ICMJE forms, all outside the submitted work: E Ros reports research grants, lecture fees, travel support and unpaid advisory membership from the California Walnut Commission, and grants or fees from pharmaceutical companies; J Salas-Salvadó reports grants, expenses and unpaid scientific committee membership from the Nut and Dried Fruit Foundation and fees or grants from Danone, Aguas Font Vella Lanjarón and Eroski; R Estruch reports grants or fees from Cerveza y Salud, Brewers of Europe, FIVIN, Novartis and Lilly; RM Lamuela-Raventós reports fees from Kao and Cerveza y Salud; X Pintó and F Arós report fees from pharmaceutical companies.
result: Mediterranean diet with extra virgin olive oil (1 litre per week per household, goal at least 4 tablespoons a day), Mediterranean diet with 30 g mixed nuts a day, or control diet (advice to reduce dietary fat), with quarterly dietary sessions. Primary end point (myocardial infarction, stroke or cardiovascular death): 96 of 2543 (3.8%), 83 of 2454 (3.4%) and 109 of 2450 (4.4%); 8.1, 8.0 and 11.2 per 1000 person-years; 5-year absolute risks 3.6%, 4.0% and 5.7%; adjusted hazard ratios 0.69 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.91) for olive oil and 0.72 (0.54 to 0.95) for nuts. The authors report an absolute difference of 1.7 to 2.1 percentage points over 5 years; the reciprocal of 2.1 points gives a number needed to treat of 48 for 5 years for the olive oil diet. Death from any cause 118, 116 and 114 (hazard ratios 0.90, 0.69 to 1.18, and 1.12, 0.86 to 1.47). Stroke 0.65 (0.44 to 0.95) and 0.54 (0.35 to 0.82); myocardial infarction 0.82 (0.52 to 1.30) and 0.76 (0.47 to 1.25). Protocol deviations not described in the 2013 report: 425 household members assigned without randomisation to the group of the member already enrolled; 467 participants at site D assigned by clinic; inconsistent use of randomisation tables at site B (593 participants). The original report was withdrawn; estimates were adjusted for baseline characteristics and propensity scores and do not rely exclusively on the assumption that all participants were randomly assigned. Excluding all 1588 participants with known or suspected deviations (5859 analysed): hazard ratios 0.71 (0.52 to 0.97) and 0.68 (0.49 to 0.95). Urinary hydroxytyrosol was measured as the adherence biomarker of the olive oil group. The oil supplied was polyphenol-rich, unlike the ordinary refined variety, which is poor in polyphenols. Fish and legume intake rose by 0.3 and 0.4 weekly servings in the Mediterranean groups against control; the authors state that the major between-group differences involved the supplemental items, extra virgin olive oil and nuts.
